title: From "I will not" to "I will"
hookLine: the warrior who said "I will not fight" gives his last words, six hundred verses later
carry: when confusion goes, "i will not" becomes "i will"
tomorrow: you know a root. can you guess a word you've never met?

cards: More than six hundred verses ago, Arjuna said na yotsya, I will not fight, and fell silent.

Since then he has asked question after question, and Krishna has talked him through action and its fruit, the self that doesn't come and go, and much more. Now, near the very end, Krishna asks him two questions.
Did you hear all this with a focused mind? Is the confusion born of not-knowing gone? And Arjuna gives his last words in the Gita.

teach.h: NASHTO MOHAH: MY CONFUSION IS GONE.
teach.b: Nashto mohah, he says. My confusion is gone. Smritir labdha: I've found my memory again, by your grace.
I stand firm, my doubts are gone.

teach.h: KARISHYE, AND THE FOG OF MOHA.
teach.b: Karishye vachanam tava: I will do as you say. Hear the words. Na yotsya, I will not, has become karishye, I will do, from kri, the root of karma.

And moha, confusion, names the fog the Gita opened in: the blind king's mamakah, mine, and the grief that dropped Arjuna's bow. Here's the big Hindu idea, said plainly. Krishna's first words called it a faint heart.
But the Gita names the deeper trouble: moha, seeing mine and theirs, taking what comes and goes for what is real. The cure isn't a pep talk.

teach.h: THE CURE: KNOWLEDGE FROM A TEACHER.
teach.b: It's knowledge, asked for and received from a teacher.
And what it gives back is smriti, memory. Many teachers read that as: not something new, but who he already was. Now the week, as one road.
The king says mamakah, mine. The warrior says teach me, and iti, falls silent. Krishna: your claim is to the action, never the fruit.
The prayer: lead me from the unreal to the real. Sukha and duhkha come and go; the self doesn't. The thunder says datta, give.

teach.h: I WILL NOT, TO I WILL.
teach.b: And the student stands up: I will. When a "won't" is really fog, the tradition's answer is to ask, to learn, and to remember who you are.

how: Many Hindus read the Gita through, chapter by chapter, and many teachers point to Arjuna's nashto mohah at the close of chapter 18 as where the whole book lands; Sanskrit learners review core words in families by root.

practice: Close the eyes and let one word from the week come back on each out-breath: mamakah, iti, karma, gamaya, sukha, datta. Then one more: karishye, I will. Don't translate; let each one arrive and go.
If you pray, end the way Arjuna did, offering what you'll do today. If not, rest in the quiet after the last one.

wordCard.voice: Two hundred core words: plain words that keep coming back. This week's: mamakah, iti, karma, gamaya, sukha, datta, and today, karishye, I will do, from kri. A week of plain words, and the Gita's whole road.
